title: A desert turned to stone
teaches: How water and wind sort grains, and how a moving dune leaves sloping layers behind

blocks.text: Drive into Zion National Park in southern Utah from the east, and one of the first landmarks you pass is a pale dome of rock called Checkerboard Mesa. Its face is scored with a grid of grooves, some running across the slope and others cutting nearly straight down, until the hill resembles a sheet of graph paper draped over stone.

blocks.caption: Checkerboard Mesa, near the east entrance of Zion.

blocks.text: The vertical grooves follow fractures known as **joints**. Near the surface, the rock expands and contracts with changes in temperature and moisture, while winter ice wedges open existing flaws until the stone splits along parallel lines. The horizontal bands follow the internal layers of the rock itself, and up close they are not level at all. Within each band run finer layers that sweep down at angles of 20 to 30 degrees and curve toward the base, before being planed off flat by the next bundle of sloping layers above, which may tilt in another direction altogether. These sloping layers are **cross-beds**, and each bounded group of them is a **set**.

Where the layers in the previous lesson settled flat on the floor of a sea or lake, these were laid down on a slope. The rock is the **Navajo Sandstone**, cemented from buried sand in the same way as the sandstones of Lesson 1. It forms both Checkerboard Mesa and the main walls of Zion Canyon, rising from the river nearly to the rim in cliffs more than 600 metres tall.

blocks.caption: Zion Canyon, cut into the Navajo Sandstone. Springdale, at the mouth of the canyon, sits more than 500 metres below the summit of Angels Landing.

options.title: Zion, Utah
options.alt: A shaded relief map of Zion Canyon, a deep north-south gorge, with Springdale at its mouth and Checkerboard Mesa to the east.

blocks.text: Piling up 600 metres of clean sand takes a vast supply, and stacking it in tilted sheets requires a mechanism quite different from slow settling in quiet water.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The cliffs of Zion, including Checkerboard Mesa, are carved from more than 600 metres of the Navajo Sandstone.
Within the sandstone are cross-beds: thin layers inclined at 20 to 30 degrees, grouped into sets that are sliced off at the top by the set above.

blocks.text: The grains themselves offer the first clue. Under a hand lens, the Navajo Sandstone consists almost entirely of quartz sand of nearly uniform size, around a fifth of a millimetre across, with almost no mud or gravel mixed in. A sediment this uniform is described as **well sorted**: whatever delivered the sand selected one narrow range of grain sizes and left everything else behind.

Both flowing water and wind sort sediment by weight. A current can lift or roll a grain only if it moves fast enough, and the larger the grain, the faster the flow must be. At any given speed, the finest particles stay suspended in the fluid, intermediate grains roll and hop along the bed, and the heaviest sit untouched. Whenever the current slackens, the coarsest grains it was carrying are the first to drop out.

blocks.caption: Six grain sizes, from clay to cobbles, in a river or in the wind.
blocks.task: Adjust the river speed to leave a bed of clean fine sand

blocks.text: In water, sorting tracks the speed of the current: a steep mountain torrent leaves cobbles and gravel on its bed, a slower lowland river deposits sand, and only still water allows mud to settle. Air, at roughly one eight-hundredth the density of water, is a far stricter filter. It can loft fine dust for thousands of kilometres, yet even a gale struggles to shift a pebble the size of a fingertip. Wind therefore drives sand along the ground in a steady bounding motion while winnowing the dust away into the atmosphere and abandoning any gravel behind.

blocks.caption: A beach sorted by wave action, with fine sand where the swash runs gently and a bank of pebbles where the surf breaks hardest.

blocks.text: Under a microscope, many grains in the Navajo Sandstone show a second feature: they are well rounded, with a dull, frosted surface like sea glass. Modern desert sands look the same. In water, the surrounding liquid slows the grains and cushions their collisions. In air, nothing softens the impact as grains strike one another thousands of times while bouncing across the ground, and the microscopic pits left by those collisions frost the quartz.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Currents of water and air sort sediment by grain size; the faster the flow, the larger the grain it can move.
Because air has a tiny fraction of the density of water, wind moves sand easily while leaving pebbles behind and carrying dust away, producing exceptionally well-sorted sand.
Grains in the Navajo Sandstone are well sorted, well rounded, and frosted by repeated collisions in air.

blocks.text: Left to blow across a supply of loose sand, wind gathers it into **dunes**. A simple dune is asymmetric, with a long, gentle windward slope and a short, steep leeward face. Wind rolls and bounces grains up the gentle back until they pass the crest, where the air slows in the shelter of the ridge and the sand drops out of the current. As sand builds up just beyond the crest, the slope oversteepens and periodically fails, sending a thin sheet of grains sliding down the front.

blocks.caption: The steep slip face of a modern sand dune, scored by small avalanches of dry sand.

blocks.text: This leeward slope is the **slip face**. Because loose, dry sand has an angle of repose between about 32 and 34 degrees, every slip face stabilises near that inclination, and each small avalanche adds a fresh sloping layer to its surface. As sand is continuously stripped from the windward back and tipped down the slip face, the entire dune migrates downwind.

blocks.caption: A dune migrating across an older sand bed. The red line marks its active slip face.
blocks.task: Predict the wind direction from the old beds, then advance time

blocks.text: Dunes commonly march in trains separated by low hollows called **troughs**, where the wind scours the ground. As a following dune advances, the trough ahead of it sweeps across the deposits of the dune in front, planing off the upper part of its slip-face layers and leaving only their curving lower toes to be buried. That is why the cross-beds in Zion dip at 20 to 30 degrees rather than the full 34 degrees of an active slip face: only the gentler lower curves survive. What remains is a vertical stack of cross-bed sets, each sliced flat at the top by the passage of the next dune. Because those layers always dip toward the leeward side, preserved cross-beds record the prevailing wind direction of the ancient desert.

blocks.caption: Cross-beds in the Navajo Sandstone. Each set of inclined layers preserves the lower part of a dune slip face, truncated by the dune that followed.

blocks.text: Steno's principle of original horizontality still applies here if you step back from the individual layers to the sets themselves. The bounding surfaces between sets, planed off as successive troughs migrated across the sand sea, were laid down nearly flat; only the internal layers within each set were deposited on a slope.

Cross-beds also work as a plumb line in deformed rocks. Because each layer curves smoothly into the floor of its set at the base and is cut off sharply at the top, you can tell at a glance which way was originally up. In mountain belts where tectonic compression has folded strata past the vertical, as in the overturned beds of Lesson 1, upside-down cross-beds curve toward the sky and end abruptly at their bases, showing that the entire sequence has been inverted.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A dune migrates downwind as sand is eroded from its gentle windward slope and avalanches down its steep slip face.
Preserved cross-beds are the lower portions of old slip faces, dipping in the direction the wind was blowing.
Because cross-beds curve into the base of a set and are sliced off at the top, they show whether a rock layer is still right-side up.

blocks.text: Currents of water in rivers and shallow seas also build ripples and dunes, and these leave cross-bedded sandstones of their own. Well into the 1970s, a minority of geologists argued that the Navajo Sandstone had accumulated on a shallow marine shelf, before several independent lines of evidence settled the case in favour of an arid land surface.

The most immediate clue is scale. Underwater ripples stand only a few centimetres high and leave cross-bed sets of the same modest thickness. River-bed dunes typically produce sets up to a metre or so thick, and while giant tidal sand waves can occasionally build larger ones, in the Navajo Sandstone sets routinely exceed 10 metres and sometimes reach more than 20 metres from base to top. Across thousands of square kilometres, only desert dunes the size of multi-storey buildings leave sets on that scale.

blocks.caption: Ripple marks formed by water in an older sandstone. Both the ripples and the cross-bed sets they leave behind are only a few centimetres high.

blocks.text: Everything at the grain scale points the same way. The quartz grains are sorted and frosted as only wind can manage, and marine fossils are absent. The only carbonate rocks within the Navajo are thin lenses of limestone and dolomite deposited in short-lived oasis ponds that formed where the water table rose above the floor of an interdune trough, and these contain freshwater crustaceans, horsetail-like plants, and vertebrate tracks. On the inclined cross-beds themselves, geologists find fossilised footprints of small early dinosaurs and crocodile relatives walking up the dry slopes of the dunes.

Taken together, the rocks record a vast Early Jurassic sand sea, or **erg**, that covered the region around 190 million years ago. Along with its neighbouring formations, the Navajo erg stretched across large parts of modern Utah, Arizona, Nevada, Idaho, Colorado, and Wyoming, forming one of the largest sand deserts in the geological record. At Zion, the cross-beds dip predominantly toward the south and southwest, recording prevailing winds that blew from the north and northeast. For hundreds of metres of loose dune sand to survive rather than blow away, the crust beneath the desert had to subside slowly over millions of years, allowing each generation of dunes to bury the toes of the last below the reach of the wind, until younger sediments sealed the deposit and mineral-rich groundwater cemented the quartz grains into stone.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Cross-bed sets tens of metres thick, frosted and wind-sorted grains, land-animal footprints, and the absence of marine fossils show that the Navajo Sandstone formed in a desert.
Around 190 million years ago, in the Early Jurassic, Zion lay within one of the largest sand seas in Earth's history.
Because the cross-beds at Zion dip south and southwest, the prevailing Jurassic winds blew from the north and northeast.

blocks.caption: Six questions on sorting, dunes, and cross-beds

items.ask: What do these sets of sloping layers in the Navajo Sandstone represent?
choices: The lower parts of dune slip faces that migrated across the desert
Horizontal beds that were tilted by tectonic folding in different directions
Parallel cooling fractures that later filled with blown sand
items.why: Each set preserves the curving lower portion of a migrating dune's slip face. Because the bounding surfaces between the sets remain nearly flat, the slope within each set must be original to the deposition of the sand rather than the result of later tilting.

items.ask: As a fast-flowing river enters a wider, gentler stretch and loses speed, which part of its sediment load settles out first?
choices: The coarsest grains it was carrying
The finest silt and clay in suspension
All grain sizes settle at the same rate
items.why: Larger, heavier grains require a higher flow velocity to keep moving, so they drop to the bed as soon as the current slackens. Fine mud remains suspended until the water is nearly still.

items.ask: Why are wind-blown desert sands almost entirely free of pebbles?
choices: Air is too low in density to lift or roll pebbles, so the wind leaves them behind
Pebbles shatter into sand grains as soon as the wind picks them up
Pebbles are carried higher in the atmosphere and deposited farther downwind
items.why: At roughly one eight-hundredth the density of water, air cannot exert enough force in normal winds to move gravel. Wind bounces sand-sized grains along the surface, blows fine dust away in suspension, and leaves pebbles behind as a stony desert pavement.

items.ask: In a sandstone cliff face, the cross-beds dip consistently toward the east. Which way was the wind blowing when those dunes formed?
choices: Cross-beds record the presence of wind, but not its direction
items.why: Cross-beds form on the leeward slip face of a dune, so they always slope downward in the downwind direction. Beds dipping east were laid down by a wind blowing toward the east.

items.ask: What process is occurring on the steep face of the dune shown here?
choices: Sand blown over the crest is avalanching down the leeward slip face
Wind is scouring sand from the trough and driving it up toward the crest
Flowing water is cutting flat layers into the side of the dune
items.why: This is the leeward slip face. Wind pushes sand up the gentler slope on the far side of the crest; once the sand builds past the angle of repose (about 32 to 34 degrees) just beyond the crest, it slides down this face in small avalanches.

items.ask: You find a sandstone containing marine bivalve shells and cross-bed sets that are 3 centimetres thick. In what environment did it most likely form?
choices: Under water, built by small current or wave ripples
In the middle of a continental sand desert
On a steep debris slope at the base of a mountain cliff
items.why: Cross-bed sets only a few centimetres thick are the product of small ripples, and the marine shells confirm that the ripples were driven by water currents rather than desert winds.

learned: Flowing water and wind sort sediment by grain size; because air is far less dense than water, wind is an especially strict sorter that moves sand while leaving gravel behind.
As dunes migrate downwind, the lower toes of their slip faces are preserved as cross-bed sets that dip in the downwind direction.
Cross-beds are sliced off at the top and curve into their base, which shows whether deformed strata are still the right way up.
The Navajo Sandstone of Zion preserves an Early Jurassic sand sea that covered much of the American West around 190 million years ago.
